Brightpearl keeps the stock and the books: Customers, stock, purchasing and invoices stay in Brightpearl. On our side sit each kitchen's guide and its prices, which you keep current in the VoiceOrder Solutions admin platform, plus every order made through the app.

Leave webstore and EDI accounts as they are: Accounts ordering through a B2B website or by EDI already reach Brightpearl with nobody typing, so keep them on that. The app is for the ones that phone instead. Calls to your office still get no order number from us; orders from the app always carry one.

Your Automation Engine rules stay as you wrote them: Nothing in your workflows changes. Once our order is in Brightpearl, whether it came by EDI, through the API or was keyed in from the emailed file, your rules route and invoice it as usual.

@graph.name: Would a Brightpearl alternative be needed for spoken orders?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Nothing in Brightpearl changes: not the stock, the price lists or the Automation Engine. What changes is what those rules receive: for a restaurant that phones today, the chef now says its order in the app, looks down the list and fixes any mistake first, rather than your team typing it from a call.

@graph.name: Is VoiceOrder Solutions better than Brightpearl?

acceptedAnswer.text: For one task, yes: letting the chef who decided an order see and fix each item before your rules act on it. Everything after that, from picking to the invoice, is Brightpearl's work, so we sit next to it and are not a Brightpearl alternative.

@graph.name: Brightpearl's automation catches exceptions. Won't it spot a mistake?

acceptedAnswer.text: Its rules can flag the orders you define, such as risky or high-value ones, so a rule can catch some mistakes, like an amount far above normal. An item that was misheard usually looks ordinary: a product that account buys anyway, in a normal amount. Our app puts each item in front of the chef before sending, so the one who knows the kitchen's needs gets a chance to catch it.

@graph.name: Couldn't our restaurant customers just order on a B2B webstore?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some will. Brightpearl can link to a separate B2B website built on an ecommerce platform, and partners sell portals and ordering apps that create Brightpearl sales orders. Other companies build ordering and AI tools on its API too, so ours is not the only way to add ordering. We built it for the chef who picks up the phone today: they speak the items, see the list and fix a wrong one before it reaches you.

@graph.name: Can the app still send a wrong order?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. The app turns speech into items from the guide, and a chef can miss a mistake or change their mind after sending. What changes is that the chef, who knows the kitchen, reads down the order before it goes, instead of hearing it read back over a call, if it is read back at all.

@graph.name: Is it linked to Brightpearl, and will my desk still type orders?

acceptedAnswer.text: Each comes from its own company, with no built-in link between them, and each supports its own software only. If Brightpearl is set up to accept orders through EDI or the API, ours can go in without anyone retyping them; the demo is where we find out. By email, the attachment shows each item the chef checked, and someone on your side enters it from that instead of from a call or a voicemail.

@graph.name: How fast is setup, and how is it priced?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most distributors are ready in 24 to 48 hours, and nobody has to change a thing in Brightpearl. Brightpearl quotes each business rather than listing prices, and we quote per distributor too. A Brightpearl replacement would shift your stock, warehouse and books to a new system, while adding us leaves every workflow you built where it is.
